items.title: Does Scaling Toward AGI Depend on What System-1 Lets System-2 Execute?
items.reason_zh: 讨论通用交互筛选、训练与推理计算分配；读到的理论并非 Harness 演化专项理论。

source_quotes.quote:
Determining which interactions to execute is a challenge that System-2 cannot resolve autonomously because assessing an interaction’s value must cost considerably less than executing it.
This necessitates the co-design of System-1 and System-2, and this work introduces the conditional interaction as a feasible co-design principle: a lightweight System-1 predicts the utility of potential interactions, the resource-intensive System-2 executes only those interactions that exceed a resource-aware threshold, and the resulting outcomes then serve to refine System-1.
Because each system shapes the other, the two must be designed together, and this Perspective asks whether such co-design is a promising path toward AGI.
Our central hypothesis posits that the density of utility-relevant interactions, denoted as ρ u \rho_{u} , rather than the sheer count of interactions alone, serves as a pivotal metric of scaling efficiency.
The co-design of System-1 and System-2, as detailed below, indicates a promising approach for scenarios where interactions are costly, exhibit uneven value, and can be anticipated. This framework is based on the premise that low-cost experiments can be conducted and foreseen effectively.

In response, we prioritize architecture over algorithm: give the executive a partner whose job is to judge, and design the two together.
This work argues that a major part of the next advance toward AGI and beyond may come from co-designing System-1 and System-2 rather than from scaling System-2 alone: specifying, training, and scaling the two as one system, where System-1 decides what System-2 executes, which executive runs it, how much it may spend, and what it keeps in memory; System-2’s outcomes are System-1’s supervision; and each is sized with the other in view ( Section 3 ).
Integrating a cheap predictor with a costly executor introduces three decisions at scale: which prompts, tasks, or requests merit rollouts, trials, or extensive thought chains ( compute ); which samples, buffers, caches, and context entries should be preserved ( storage ); and how costly outcomes should adjust the inexpensive judgment that allocated them ( feedback ).

This work proposes conditional interaction as a coupling mechanism that allocates interactions based on predicted utility, explicitly optimizing to avoid those predicted to fall below a certain threshold.
This perspective applies to diverse applications, including online prompt selection in reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) ( Qu et al., 2026a ) , task selection in embodied agents ( Qu et al., 2025 ) , model routing, and adaptive inference ( Li et al., 2026 ) ( Section 2.3 ).
The same pattern applies in a deployed system, where the ledger records inference compute and real-world actions rather than gradient updates ( Snell et al., 2024 ) .
The transfer focuses on the decision pattern and the scope is intentionally confined to situations with a reliable utility predictor, as this principle does not substitute exploration when the predictor is uncertain ( Section 2.4 ).

source_quotes.quote: Following common practice in prompt optimization ( Pryzant et al., 2023 ; Ye et al., 2024 ) , training examples provide feedback for prompt updates, and validation performance selects prompts along the optimization trajectory. The feedback and selection mechanisms used within prompt search depend on the underlying optimizer.

Existing prompt optimizers ( Zhou et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Pryzant et al., 2023 ; Ye et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) can account for dependencies among agents when updating the prompt collection 𝐩 \mathbf{p} in Eq. ( 1 ). Nevertheless, shared coordination and agent-specific execution remain expressed within per-agent prompts. We instead make them distinct optimization targets: a shared component specifies how agents collaborate, and local components specify how they execute their respective tasks. This separation allows a coordination update to be applied consistently across agents while execution updates remain specific to individual roles.

Here, 𝒪 ⁡ ( p , 𝒞 , Φ , 𝒟 ) \mathcal{O}(p;\,\mathcal{C},\,\Phi,\,\mathcal{D}) updates the target prompt while keeping 𝒞 \mathcal{C} fixed. The full MAS f 𝒮 f_{\mathcal{S}} is run on 𝒟 train \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}} , and failures under ℳ \mathcal{M} provide feedback for candidate updates. Each coordinator iterate is evaluated on 𝒟 val \mathcal{D}_{\text{val}} with the initial executors fixed. We select p C ⋆ p_{C}^{\star} from the initial prompt and all iterates according to the highest system-level validation score J J .

Training feedback is collected from the full MAS under p C ⋆ p_{C}^{\star} and the executor context used for the update, and the executor prompt is selected by validation scores. Agents outside ℐ \mathcal{I} retain their initial prompts. The choice ℐ = ∅ \mathcal{I}=\emptyset gives coordinator-only optimization, while ℐ = { 1 , … , N } \mathcal{I}=\{1,\ldots,N\} permits optimization of every executor. The executor subsets are described in § B.2 . Algorithm 1 summarizes the default procedure.

Since the document benchmarks lack dedicated training sets, we partition their test sets into document-level train/validation/test splits of 10/10/80 using a fixed seed. Baseline scores on our test splits are close to those on the original test sets (Appendix A.1 ). We evaluate answers with GPT-5-mini following the LLM-as-judge protocol of ( Han et al., 2025a ) (Appendix C.1 ). We follow MASPO ( Wang et al., 2026b ) for mathematical reasoning and code generation settings. For video understanding, we follow LongVideoAgent ( Liu et al., 2026 ) , retaining its test set and reserving 50 questions from its training set for validation.

items.title: RoboArchitect: Automating the Design of Robotic Agents with Persistent Memory
items.reason_zh: 冻结机器人策略；编码模型用执行轨迹诊断失败并修订控制程序，经训练集反馈选择后用于未见场景和任务。

source_quotes.quote:
RoboArchitect optimizes the harness around a frozen policy, as illustrated in Fig. 2 .
It starts from a harness that passes the policy’s actions through unchanged and repeats an empirical optimization loop: the harness runs on the training episodes, a coding model observes the recorded rollouts, diagnoses the failures and refines the harness.
These “training” episodes serve only to optimize the harness: no weights are updated , and the final harness is evaluated on separate held-out episodes ( Section 4.1 ).
Over iterations, the harness grows into a highly performant robotic agent that, as needed, follows the policy, consults auxiliary tools, or commands the arm directly, and it can carry experience in a persistent memory.
Below, we describe its key components.

Optimization loop. The optimization follows the same trial-and-error loop as a human engineer ( Section 1 ).
Every evaluation logs complete trajectory traces, including per-step camera frames, the robot’s readings, and all model and tool outputs.
A coding model reviews these execution traces from the current harness, diagnoses failure modes, and proposes a candidate harness revision, where it may follow the policy, invoke any of the tools, or command the arm programmatically.
The automated optimization loop thus settles the balance between policy and programmatic control ( Section 4.2 ).
The candidate is then re-evaluated on the same training set ( Section 4.1 ) and accepted only if its performance surpasses that of the current harness, following the empirical validation in prior work on self-improving agents ( Zhang et al., 2026b ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) .
We thus ensure a monotonic optimization trajectory on the training set, capped at a maximum number of iterations ( Section 4.1 ). We compare iterative refinement with a single-attempt automated agent design in Section 4.2 .
Held-out evaluation protocols. Every harness is evaluated on held-out episodes never seen during the harness’s optimization ( i.e., “training”), under the following protocols:

(1) Unseen scenes .
Training and held-out splits share identical tasks but differ in initial scene arrangements and layouts ( Fig. 9 , left). The evolved harness must generalize beyond specific object positions or spatial configurations.

(2) Unseen tasks .
Training and held-out splits contain different tasks that share underlying manipulation skills ( Fig. 9 , right). The evolved harness must generalize at the skill level rather than memorizing task-specific routines.

Importantly, these memories are data structures within the designed robot agent , not the coding model’s own context: they accumulate information during the agent’s rollouts and persist across episodes at execution time.
As shown in Table 3 , the harnesses actively consult their memory several times per episode on average, and over 90% of these reads are actionable , that is, they successfully find a stored entry, even on held-out episodes unseen during harness optimization.
Because every evaluation starts with an empty memory to be accumulated, these entries’ designs effectively carry over to held-out episodes and remain highly useful.

Sim-to-real transfer. All evaluations run in simulation.
Because our harness reads only the standard input space ( e.g., camera images, depth and the robot’s own readings), its interface should carry over to a real robot.
Testing our simulation-evolved harnesses on real robots and investigating the number of further improvement iterations on a real deployment are future work.
